name: Dhruva
role: Child devotee of Vishnu linked to the Pole Star
summary: Dhruva is a young prince in the Puranas who walked into the forest to find Vishnu. Hindu tradition links him with the Pole Star, the one point in the night sky that seems never to move.
about: Dhruva appears in the Vishnu Purana and the Bhagavata Purana as the son of King Uttanapada and Queen Suniti. His name means fixed or unshakeable. According to these texts, when he was about five he was turned away from his father's lap by his stepmother Suruchi, and his mother Suniti advised him to seek Narayana. The sage Narada is said to have taught him a mantra and a way to meditate beside the Yamuna at Madhuvana. The Bhagavata describes months of growing austerity before Vishnu appeared. In the Vishnu Purana version Dhruva asks for knowledge of a hymn rather than a reward. Tradition says he was then given the place of the Pole Star, called dhruva-pada, steady even through the dissolution of the world. He ruled for many years, and the Bhagavata later says he rose to Vishnu's abode. At Hindu weddings the couple is often shown the Pole Star as a sign of steadiness.
kidSummary: Dhruva is a small prince in Hindu stories who wanted to find God after feeling hurt. The old texts say he went to the forest, practised patiently, and was given a place as the star that never moves. Many families show it to newly married couples as a sign of staying steady.

story.title: A hurt little prince
story.text: In the Puranas, young Dhruva tried to climb onto his father's lap but his stepmother told him he could not. He ran to his mother Suniti, who comforted him.

story.title: A gentle suggestion
story.text: Suniti told him to turn to Narayana, the lord Vishnu, for help. Dhruva decided to go to the forest to find him.

story.title: Meeting Narada
story.text: The sage Narada said it was too hard for a child. Dhruva stayed firm, so Narada taught him a mantra and the way to meditate beside the Yamuna.

story.title: Patient practice
story.text: The Bhagavata Purana describes months of fasting and slowly stilling the breath, until Dhruva stood as still as a pillar. Vishnu then appeared to him.

story.title: A place in the sky
story.text: In the Vishnu Purana, Dhruva asked only for a hymn to praise Vishnu. The Bhagavata says he later felt he had asked for too little. Either way, he was granted a steady, lasting place, which tradition names the Pole Star, the star that never seems to move.

teaches: Patience and practice can change your life
Be steady like the Pole Star

facts.text: In the Bhagavata story, Dhruva's stepmother told him he could only sit on his father's lap if he were born from her, a taunt that sent the five-year-old into the forest.
Narada's first advice was to go home, but Dhruva answered that he wanted a place higher than anyone had won in the three worlds, even his father and grandfather, and asked for an honest path to it.
The Bhagavata counts his penance by months: fruit every third day, then dry leaves every sixth, then water every ninth, then air every twelfth, then standing on one leg.
The text says his concentration grew so strong that the universe's breath seemed to stop, and the devas hurried to Vishnu for help.
The Mahabharata calls the pole star dhruva nakshatra, though scholars note that Polaris was still several degrees from the celestial pole when that epic was likely compiled.

In the Vishnu Purana's telling, Dhruva wants no throne or heaven, only knowledge of a hymn to praise Vishnu. One summary adds that he had remembered Vishnu so long that he forgot what he had come to ask.

After a Yaksha killed his half-brother Uttama, Dhruva marched on Alakapuri and fought until his anger fell on innocents; Manu told him to stop. The Yaksha king Kubera then offered a boon, and Dhruva asked only to keep his devotion to Vishnu.
As he climbed aboard, the Bhagavata says Dhruva stepped on the head of Death, shown as a person, a picture of rising beyond fear of dying.
Dhruva worried about leaving his mother Suniti behind, and the Bhagavata says Vishnu's attendants showed him she was travelling on another aerial car.
The Bhagavata says Dhruva's abode is circled by the sun, moon and stars, like bulls walking round a central pole.
At a Hindu wedding, the couple look at the Pole Star on the first evening in their new home, and the husband recites a prayer asking for a steady household.
In the Bhagavata, Dhruva stood before Vishnu with folded hands but could not find words, so Vishnu touched his conch to the boy, and Dhruva at once understood and spoke a hymn of praise.
Offered anything he wished, Dhruva later felt he had asked for too little, like a poor man who, offered anything by an emperor, begs for a few broken grains of rice, says the Bhagavata.
The Bhagavata says that on Dhruva's return his father leapt down from his chariot to hug him in tears, and even his stepmother Suruchi embraced him and blessed him with a long life.
The Bhagavata pictures Dhruva's balancing on one leg as so heavy that half the earth sank beneath his toe, swaying like a boat that carries a walking elephant.
After Dhruva left, the Bhagavata says his father Uttanapada was full of regret, picturing the boy hungry in the forest and wishing he had embraced him when he reached for his lap.
Dhruva went home to a warm welcome and was crowned at just six years old. He then ruled fairly for many decades, says the Dhruva article.
After the Yaksha war, the Yaksha king Kuvera told Dhruva that the Yakshas had not truly killed his brother, nor had Dhruva truly killed them, because time moves everything, says the Bhagavata.
Narada told Dhruva that chanting the twelve-syllable mantra Om Namo Bhagavate Vasudevaya for seven nights could let a devotee see perfected beings flying across the sky, says the Bhagavata.

When Dhruva's life ended, the Bhagavata says a shining aerial car came down like a falling full moon, with two attendants of Vishnu named Nanda and Sunanda, who said his penance at five had won a place no ancestor had reached.

The Dhruva article notes that in the Vishnu Purana, others might have asked for riches, heaven or even liberation, but Dhruva had no wish of his own, and that lack of desire is the idea behind his lasting seat, dhruva-pada.
On reaching the Yaksha city of Alakapuri, Dhruva blew his conch, and the Bhagavata says the sound rolled across the sky and frightened the Yaksha women.

quiz.q: Which star is Dhruva linked with?
quiz.why: Tradition gives Dhruva the Pole Star as his seat.

quiz.q: What does the name Dhruva mean?
Which sage taught Dhruva a mantra?
quiz.why: Narada is said to have guided him.

quiz.q: Where did Dhruva do his practice?
quiz.why: Narada sent him to Madhuvana on the Yamuna.

quiz.q: Whose lap was Dhruva not allowed to sit on?
quiz.why: His stepmother stopped him sitting on King Uttanapada's lap.
